text: [ios_base standard streams](../../../core/libs/prx/libc/src/LocaleSupport.cpp) (libc) `_Addstd` queues the stream in the standard stream table of Dinkumware [ios.cpp](https://github.com/ganboing/crt.vc12/blob/master/src/ios.cpp) (`stdstr`, `stdopens`, `_Addstd`, `_Ios_base_dtor`): it takes the first of slots 1 to 7 that is free or already holds the stream, and slot 8 (`NSTDSTR`) when none is, so slot 8 is shared by every stream past the first seven and registration never fails. It stores the 1-based slot index in the guest `IosBase::standardStream` (Dinkumware's `_Stdstr`, where 0 means not a standard stream) and counts the stream objects registered per slot; registering the same stream again reuses its slot and raises its count. Measured on a PS5 (firmware 13.60) from a homebrew payload calling the system `libSceLibcInternal` export: in a process whose own standard streams already hold slots 1 to 7, twelve distinct streams and a repeated one all get 8, written as a 64-bit value at offset 0x8 with no other byte of the object touched; the assignment of slots 1 to 7 to fresh streams is not observable there and follows VC12. The counts are `int`, not VC12's `char`, and the registration and the destructor lock the table where VC12 locks only `_Addstd`; a slot index past the table throws in the destructor instead of indexing out of bounds. The destructor decrements its slot's count and suppresses the rest of the destruction while the count stays positive, as `_Ios_base_dtor` does, and the slots of destroyed streams keep their pointer and stay reserved for that stream, as `stdstr` does. The streams themselves are destroyed by the title's own code as it registers them through `__cxa_atexit`; when the last reference closes, the unsupported stream storage and callback cleanup is still the throw it was and the locale is released as for a non-standard stream.

The payload goes under the quiet bit with the sign, as in gdtoa's [`strtod`](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/release/11.0.0/contrib/gdtoa/strtod.c#L316-L328). `strtof`, `wcstof`, `strtold` and `wcstold` return the positive default quiet NaN (`0x7fc00000`; exponent `0x7fff`, significand `0xc000000000000000`) whatever the sign and the sequence, and consume a sequence of letters, digits and underscores up to its closing parenthesis. The console's `libSceLibcInternal.sprx`, called from a payload process on a PS5 (firmware 12.70), gives these results for the 64 NaN inputs tried through `strtod` and `strtof`, 50 of them also through `strtold` and `wcstod`, and 18 through `wcstof` and `wcstold`, and, through `strtod`, for `nan(1 2)` and for `nan( ` followed by NUL and `)`; that a title's own `libc.prx` does the same is assumed. In `hexnan`, a blank after a payload digit, while a 32-bit word of the payload is still free, starts a blank skip that has no NUL check, so when only blanks follow up to the terminating NUL the console's `strtod` reads past it: `nan(1 ` followed by NUL and `)` consumes the `)` after the NUL, so the result depends on the bytes after the string, and here that case throws. A blank right after `nan(` is skipped with a NUL check, and the console stopped at the NUL there

text: [syslog](../../../core/libs/prx/libc/src/Syslog.cpp) (libc) writes each message to `stderr` as `[syslog:<priority>] <message>`, with a newline added when missing, instead of sending it to the console's system log. Priority and facility handling follow FreeBSD's `vsyslog`: `%m` expands to the guest errno's message, unknown bits are reported (as priority 0x23, since FreeBSD passes `LOG_ERR|LOG_CONS|LOG_PERROR|LOG_PID` as the priority) and masked, a missing facility becomes `LOG_USER` or the facility set by `openlog`, and errno is preserved. `openlog` applies its identity and `LOG_PID`; a null identity retains the previous one, and a valid nonzero facility replaces the default. `closelog` clears the identity but retains the options and facility, as in FreeBSD 11; when no identity is set, FreeBSD falls back to the program name, which this backend does not emit. `LOG_PERROR` has no extra effect because stderr is the emulated log sink; `LOG_NDELAY`/`LOG_ODELAY`, `LOG_NOWAIT` and `LOG_CONS` have no daemon, child or console backend to control. `setlogmask` follows [FreeBSD 11](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/8d2708de5d6112a492744d367cfdfb8fd219227a/lib/libc/gen/syslog.c): the process-wide mask defaults to 0xff, zero queries it, and nonzero values replace it; masked messages are skipped before formatting, including the unknown-priority diagnostic. The console's mask behaviour is unverified

The console's `y0f`, `y1f` and `ynf` raise none either, unlike [ours](../../../core/libs/prx/libc/src/Math.cpp), which raise `FE_DIVBYZERO` at ±0. The order wraps at 32 bits as on the console: `jn(1 << 30, x)` never returns for 2^-29 <= |x| < 2^30

text: [localtime, mktime](../../../core/libs/prx/libc/src/Time.cpp) (libc) on Windows convert through the CRT's `localtime_s` and `mktime`, which accept about 1970 to January 3001 UTC and apply the CRT's daylight-saving rule. A time outside that range is converted a whole number of 400-year Gregorian cycles away, where the calendar repeats, so it gets the rule the CRT applies to that year and not the zone's historical one. On macOS `mktime` converts through the host's `mktime`, which refuses every year before 1900. A local time before 1900 is instead solved for directly: the offset `localtime_r` gives for a candidate time, which follows the zone's history (local mean time before its first transition), is subtracted from the local fields, and the step is repeated until the offset holds. `tm_isdst` is not consulted there, so a time with `tm_isdst` set where the zone had no daylight offset is taken as standard time. FreeBSD's [`time1`](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/stable/11/contrib/tzcode/stdtime/localtime.c#L2036) would instead shift it by the difference between one of the zone's daylight types and a standard one. `gmtime` converts every time whose year fits an `int` on both hosts.

text: On macOS the [write watch](../../../core/libs/prx/libc/src/GuestWriteWatch.cpp) write-protects watched pages and records the first write to each from a SIGBUS/SIGSEGV handler, because macOS has no counterpart to `userfaultfd` write-protect or `MEM_WRITE_WATCH`. The protection is real, so: - a system call that writes into a protected page fails with `EFAULT` instead of faulting. `GuestArena::HostWrite` lifts the protection for the calls it brackets (file reads and socket receives); a host call that writes guest memory without it (`clock_gettime` and the like into a watched page) fails; - code that changes the protection of watched pages, or maps over them, has to call `GuestWriteWatchProtectionChanged`, and code that asks the kernel for a page's protection has to ask `GuestWriteWatchProtection` first, since a watched page is read-only between a collection and the next write. Nothing calls either yet: the macOS memory paths are not in the tree; - the handler is installed when libc loads and passes other faults to the handler installed before it. A handler installed later has to do the same.

name: libc.L62
text: [Guest time conversions](../../../core/libs/prx/libc/src/Time.cpp) rewrite the host process `TZ` when a guest changes its own `TZ`, so other host consumers of that variable (including libSceRtc local time) shift too; code outside libc does not take the zone lock. Zone syntax follows the host C runtime, not FreeBSD: Windows only accepts the `std offset [dst]` form, treats an empty guest `TZ` as `UTC0` and reads `:Europe/Berlin` as an abbreviation (for example `rop`); only Linux honours zone file names. If the guest accepts a `TZ` value that the host rejects (on Windows, for example, one longer than the host environment limit), conversions throw `std::runtime_error`. A `tm_zone` saved before a `TZ` change can refer to storage now holding the new zone name, changing `%Z` output.

name: libc.L65
text: Windows direct-memory backing reserves a paging-file section. A [direct memory page](../../../core/libs/prx/libc/include/WindowsMappings.hpp) mapped at one guest address is private write-watched memory at that address and is not committed in the section; a page mapped at a second address moves its whole resident run into the section (committed there) and every address becomes a view of it, tracked by write protection. An unmapped resident page that is not all zeros is kept in a private reservation until it is mapped again. Committed section contents remain across unmap/remap and are released when the backing and its remaining views are destroyed. A host import alias over part of a resident run is refused. Linux retains its existing backing. Peak gameplay memory and Windows versions other than the tested host remain unverified.

name: libc.L66
text: Stable Windows resident runs of at least 256 KiB use temporary read-only protection for clean write-watch proofs. The first CPU write restores the logical protection of the whole run; that run remains on native write watching until it is remapped, so repeatedly rewritten runs stay writable. Native kernel writes into guest buffers must hold [GuestArena::HostWrite](../../../core/libs/prx/libc/include/GuestArena.hpp), as shared views already require: an unbracketed WinAPI ReadFile can fail with ERROR_NOACCESS while the resident proof is armed. Guest read, pread and socket receive paths already bracket their destinations. GPU host-import access suppresses resident rearming without inventing shared-page stores. This is a host integration requirement, not a change to guest logical protection.

name: libc.L70
text: [Closed standard descriptors](../../../core/libs/prx/libc/src/StandardStreams.cpp) (libc) - on Linux and macOS, a descriptor 0, 1 or 2 that is closed when libc loads is opened on `/dev/null` (read-only for 0, write-only for 1 and 2) by a static initializer of libc, which runs before the libraries that depend on libc initialize and before the title starts. Within libc this relies on no static initializer opening a descriptor before it, which `guest_closed_standard_descriptors` checks. glibc does the same for set-user-ID programs ([`check_fds.c`](https://sourceware.org/git/?p=glibc.git;a=blob;f=csu/check_fds.c)). Without it the first descriptor a library opens, the write watch's `userfaultfd` for one, becomes the guest's standard input or output. What the console gives a title as its standard descriptors is not measured, and on Windows a process started without standard handles is not handled.

Its CRT owns application allocator initialization and finalization; HLE retains the module until process exit. Partial or mixed providers throw. This avoids reinitializing an allocator already used by SDK startup; console behavior and other host platforms remain unverified.

name: libc.L95
text: On macOS the [guest arena](../../../core/libs/prx/libc/src/GuestArena.cpp) finds host regions with `mach_vm_region` and reserves the rest with a fixed `mach_vm_map`, which fails instead of replacing, as macOS has no `/proc/self/maps` or `MAP_FIXED_NOREPLACE`. The kernel keeps the range up to 0x70_0000_0000 unmappable for every process (max protection none). It starts at 0x10_0000_0000 on macOS 26.5 (M1 Pro, arm64 and x86_64 under Rosetta) and at 0xF_C000_0000 on macOS 27 (27.0.1 on an M4 Pro, arm64 and x86_64 under Rosetta; 27.2 on an M2 Max, arm64). With dyld and the Rosetta runtime near 0x2_0200_0000 and 0x3_0400_0000, a guest mapping fixed inside those ranges fails where the console places it; mappings without a fixed address are placed around them.

name: libkernel.L36
text: [AMM map, map direct and unmap](../../../core/libs/prx/libkernel/Apr/src/Apr.cpp) (libSceAmpr) - signatures and the protection mask (CPU, GPU, AMPR and ACP read and write) taken from the [ampr_emu](https://github.com/drakmor/ampr_emu) reimplementation, which hands the remaining checks and the mapping to the console kernel; the mapper model taken from [PS5PCEM](https://github.com/iStark/PS5PCEM): `sceAmprAmmGiveDirectMemory` usage 1 gives the allocated direct memory to the pool plain maps take pages from, usage 0 only allocates it. Not confirmed on a title. The AMM virtual address ranges are a 256 GiB range (PPSA02015 places its heaps 64 GiB above the start of the range, so 32 GiB is too small, and reached 84 GiB above it in its first 159 s; KytyPS5 reports 512 GiB, but every 64 GiB-aligned 544 GiB window in the guest arena covers 448 to 608 GiB, and on Windows one host thread stack there is enough to block it) and a 32 GiB multimap range reserved on first use at the top of the guest arena with the start on a 64 GiB boundary (PPSA02015 tells its pool pointers from its heap pointers by address bits 28 to 35, which needs such a start for its layout), above the addresses that maps without `MAP_FIXED` are given lowest first and that titles derive their next hints from; the console's addresses are not known (ampr_emu takes them from `sceKernelMapperGetParam`), and a reservation that cannot be made there throws. Maps outside them throw. Addresses, sizes and direct offsets must be 16 KiB aligned. The memory type and the GPU mask are ignored, AMPR and ACP access maps as CPU access, unmapped pages go back to the pool and stay reserved. Submission runs the buffer before returning, the submit result is always 0 and a failing command throws; the AMM measures return errors sign-extended, as ampr_emu does. A map returns its target to the reservation before releasing the old pages, so pool exhaustion leaves that target reserved; mapping failure also restores the reservation before returning newly taken pages to the pool. The console's map failure and rollback behavior is unverified. `sceAmprAmmGetVirtualAddressRanges` throws for a null output

name: libkernel.L35
text: [APR gather and scatter reads](../../../core/libs/prx/libkernel/Apr/src/Apr.cpp) (libSceAmpr) - signatures, argument checks and the read cursor taken from the [ampr_emu](https://github.com/drakmor/ampr_emu) reimplementation, not confirmed on a title: each read leaves the file, the next file offset and the next destination; a gather reads that file at a new offset into the next destination, a scatter continues in the file into a new destination, a gather-scatter takes both. name: libkernel.L130
text: [setitimer](../../../core/libs/prx/libkernel/System/src/Signals.cpp) (libkernel) follows FreeBSD's `sys_setitimer` and `kern_setitimer`: `EINVAL` for timers other than `ITIMER_REAL`, `ITIMER_VIRTUAL` and `ITIMER_PROF`, and for a value, or the interval of a non-zero value, with a negative field, `tv_usec` of 1000000 or more, or more than `INT32_MAX / 2` seconds; a null value reads the timer as `getitimer` does, with `EFAULT` when the output is null too. `ITIMER_REAL` shares the timer thread of `alarm`, which clears its interval: a zero value disarms it, the previous value is returned, and each expiry re-arms it by `it_interval`. With `SIG_IGN` an expiry is dropped. With `SIGALRM` blocked it is left on the pending set of `sigtimedwait`, as `kern_psignal` does, where `sigwait`, `sigtimedwait` and `sigwaitinfo` take it; unblocking it runs a guest handler on the unblocking thread, and with the default disposition exits the process with status 142. Unblocked, the default disposition exits the process with status 142 and a handler throws, since guest `SIGALRM` handlers are never run from the timer thread. The value is not raised to `tick / 16` as `itimerfix` does, and an interval below 1 ms throws, since the console's `hz`, and so that rounding, is unknown (1 ms covers any `hz` of 63 or more). `ITIMER_VIRTUAL` and `ITIMER_PROF` throw when armed, as process CPU time is not accounted, and read and disarm as zero. PPSA99420 imports it and fails to load without it

name: libkernel.L191
text: [Socket descriptor numbers](../../../core/libs/prx/libkernel/Socket/src/Udp.cpp) (libkernel, libSceNet) - `socket`, `accept`, `socketpair`, `dup`, `sceNetSocket` and `sceNetAccept` take the lowest free number of the host descriptor table that files use, as FreeBSD 11.4 `fdalloc` takes the lowest free entry of the one process table (`kern_descrip.c`), so every number stays below `FD_SETSIZE` (1024) while fewer than 1024 descriptors are open. The number holds a zero-access `NUL` handle on Windows and a duplicate of the host socket on Linux, and the socket tables map it to the socket. The host table also holds the runtime's own files, so the numbers differ from the console's; the first number `socket` and `sceNetSocket` return on a console and its `getdtablesize` are not measured. Paths that bypass the socket tables see the placeholder: libc `fdopen` on a socket opens it, and libkernel `close` of a libSceNet socket releases the number but leaves the libSceNet socket open. Palworld (PPSA23126), The Mound (PPSA26223) and Dying Light 2 (PPSA02262) set socket bits in a 1024-bit `fd_set`

name: libkernel.L199

A connected stream socket keeps its host `EISCONN` answer. Known gaps: on an already connected datagram socket `connect` to port 0 keeps the old peer, where FreeBSD's `soconnect()` disconnects first and then fails with 49; `sendto` and `sendmsg` to port 0 are sent, where `udp_output()` fails with 49 on the unbound path but FreeBSD can send to port 0 from a socket bound to a specific address and port. name: libkernel.L154
text: [sceKernelRaiseException](../../../core/libs/prx/libkernel/System/src/Exception.cpp) on Linux sends the host SIGUSR1, which the library takes over, to the target thread, so the handler runs wherever the thread was interrupted, emulator code included. On the console kernel objects are system calls and libthr defers signals while a thread holds its internal locks; here a handler that needs a host lock the interrupted code holds deadlocks, and a thread that the handler keeps waiting keeps its host locks. Host waits resume after the handler. The host calls Linux does not restart end early: sleeps that do not retry return before their time, and the poll of `sceNetEpollWait` and socket calls with a send or receive timeout return `EINTR` to the guest

name: libkernel.L197
text: [getsockopt, setsockopt](../../../core/libs/prx/libkernel/Socket/src/SocketOptions.cpp) (libkernel) on a guest socket handle the SOL_SOCKET level, `TCP_NODELAY` and `IPV6_V6ONLY`, after FreeBSD 11.4's [`sosetopt` and `sogetopt`](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/release/11.4.0/sys/kern/uipc_socket.c): `SO_REUSEADDR`, `SO_KEEPALIVE`, `SO_DONTROUTE`, `SO_BROADCAST`, `SO_OOBINLINE` and `SO_LINGER` act on the host socket, and `SO_ERROR`, `SO_TYPE`, `SO_ACCEPTCONN`, `SO_SNDBUF` and `SO_RCVBUF` are read. A boolean option reads back as its own bit, as FreeBSD returns `so_options & option`. Winsock does not clear a socket's pending error when it is read, so on Windows the library reports a pending error once and shows it again only after a new `connect`; a second failure with the same code on the same socket without a `connect` in between would be hidden. `SO_SNDBUF` and `SO_RCVBUF` read the host's value, which is not the size FreeBSD reports (Linux doubles it). `SO_NOSIGPIPE` is kept per socket and reads back as its bit. On Linux a `send`, `sendto`, `sendmsg` or `write` on that socket passes `MSG_NOSIGNAL` to the host, as [`kern_sendit`](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/8c639945a44588f6cfdddfb057bb5aad88735da0/sys/kern/uipc_syscalls.c#L890-L895) and [`soo_write`](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/8c639945a44588f6cfdddfb057bb5aad88735da0/sys/kern/sys_socket.c#L147-L151) leave out the signal. An accepted socket takes it from its listener, as [`sonewconn`](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/8c639945a44588f6cfdddfb057bb5aad88735da0/sys/kern/uipc_socket.c#L603) copies the options. `SO_NBIO` (`0x1200`) is the console's own option, not FreeBSD's. It switches the socket between blocking and non-blocking as `FIONBIO` does and reads back as 0 or 1, as `sceNetSetsockopt` and `sceNetGetsockopt` treat it here; what the console reads back for it is not measured. `TCP_NODELAY` (`IPPROTO_TCP`, 1) is set on the host socket and reads back as `TF_NODELAY` (4), as [`tcp_default_ctloutput`](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/8c639945a44588f6cfdddfb057bb5aad88735da0/sys/netinet/tcp_usrreq.c#L1860-L1861) returns it. The `IPPROTO_TCP` level on a datagram or `AF_UNIX` socket fails with `EINVAL`, as [`ip_ctloutput`](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/8c639945a44588f6cfdddfb057bb5aad88735da0/sys/netinet/ip_output.c#L943-L944) and [`uipc_ctloutput`](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/8c639945a44588f6cfdddfb057bb5aad88735da0/sys/kern/uipc_usrreq.c#L1228-L1229) answer it, and an accepted socket takes `TCP_NODELAY` through the host. `SO_SNDTIMEO` and `SO_RCVTIMEO` follow [`sosetopt`](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/8c639945a44588f6cfdddfb057bb5aad88735da0/sys/kern/uipc_socket.c#L2657-L2689) and [`sogetopt`](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/8c639945a44588f6cfdddfb057bb5aad88735da0/sys/kern/uipc_socket.c#L2846-L2850). A 16-byte `timeval` with a negative field or 1000000 microseconds or more fails with `EDOM`, and more than `INT32_MAX` seconds becomes the longest wait. The value is kept and read back through FreeBSD's 32.32 fixed-point conversion ([`tvtosbt`, `sbttotv`](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/8c639945a44588f6cfdddfb057bb5aad88735da0/sys/sys/time.h#L178-L286)), so half a second reads back as 499999 microseconds and one microsecond as 0. A `recv`, `recvfrom`, `recvmsg`, `read` or `readv`, and a `send`, `sendto`, `sendmsg`, `write` or `writev`, on a blocking socket then waits that long for the host to report the socket readable or writable, and fails with `EWOULDBLOCK`; a call with `MSG_DONTWAIT` does not wait. An accepted socket takes both from its listener ([`sonewconn`](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/8c639945a44588f6cfdddfb057bb5aad88735da0/sys/kern/uipc_socket.c#L629-L630)). The wait covers only the first transfer: once the socket is writable the host send runs without a limit, where FreeBSD stops a send that cannot finish and returns the bytes sent so far, and a receive whose data another thread takes between the wait and the host call blocks again. `sendfile` ignores the send timeout. The host wait has millisecond steps, so a shorter timeout lasts up to a millisecond longer. A null value fails with `EINVAL`, where FreeBSD's [`kern_setsockopt`](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/8c639945a44588f6cfdddfb057bb5aad88735da0/sys/kern/uipc_syscalls.c#L1414-L1415) returns `EFAULT`. `IPV6_V6ONLY` (`IPPROTO_IPV6`, 27) on an `AF_INET6` socket is set on the host socket and reads back as 0 or 1, after FreeBSD's [`ip6_ctloutput`](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/8c639945a44588f6cfdddfb057bb5aad88735da0/sys/netinet6/ip6_output.c#L1716-L1732): a value that is not exactly an `int` fails with `EINVAL` ([L1572](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/8c639945a44588f6cfdddfb057bb5aad88735da0/sys/netinet6/ip6_output.c#L1572)), as does setting it on a bound socket, which the host refuses too. `socket` turns it on for every `AF_INET6` socket, as FreeBSD's default `net.inet6.ip6.v6only` does, and Java turns it off on the sockets it opens: Java 25 Advanced Network (PPSA99871) stops at `java.net.SocketException: Protocol not available` without it. The `IPPROTO_IPV6` level on an `AF_INET` or `AF_UNIX` socket fails with `EINVAL`, as `ip_ctloutput` and `uipc_ctloutput` answer it. Every other SOL_SOCKET option (`SO_DEBUG`, `SO_USELOOPBACK`, `SO_REUSEPORT` and `SO_TIMESTAMP`, which FreeBSD stores, the low-water marks among them; PPSA99871 sets `SO_REUSEPORT` and carries on when it fails), every other `IPPROTO_TCP` option (`TCP_MAXSEG`, `TCP_KEEPIDLE`, `TCP_KEEPINTVL` and `TCP_KEEPCNT` among them), every other `IPPROTO_IPV6` option ([L1928-L1929](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/8c639945a44588f6cfdddfb057bb5aad88735da0/sys/netinet6/ip6_output.c#L1928-L1929), [L2158-L2159](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/8c639945a44588f6cfdddfb057bb5aad88735da0/sys/netinet6/ip6_output.c#L2158-L2159)) and the `IPPROTO_IP` level fail with `ENOPROTOOPT`. None of this was measured on a console.

name: libkernel.L206
text: [pause, sigsuspend, sigwait, sigwaitinfo](../../../core/libs/prx/libkernel/System/src/Signals.cpp) (libkernel) take the pending set of `sigtimedwait` instead of throwing. `pause` waits for a pending signal that is not blocked and whose disposition can be delivered, runs its handler on the calling thread and returns -1 with `EINTR`; an ignored signal is discarded and the wait continues, and it never returns for a signal whose handler cannot run. A signal whose registered handler has `SA_SIGINFO` still throws, and one whose disposition is the default action and that has no host equivalent (every signal except 2, 4, 6, 8, 11 and 15) is neither delivered nor discarded: it stays pending until a wait takes it, where FreeBSD runs the default action, which terminates the process for most of them. A pending `SIGALRM` with the default disposition exits the process with status 142 once it is unblocked, as FreeBSD's default action does. PPSA68091, PPSA99169, PPSA99420 and PPSA97358 import them and fail to load without them. PPSA68091 calls `pause` at one site (0x8F7266), in a loop that waits while a global holds another thread's `errno` address. PPSA99169 only stores the address of `pause` in a table of symbol addresses (0x30DB1). PPSA99420 calls `pause` at 0x3BD80F6 and 0x3C9E220, `sigwait` at 0x3C9E4C7 and `sigwaitinfo` at 0x3C9E588. PPSA97358 calls `sigwait` from QEMU's `sigwait_compat` thread ([compatfd.c](https://github.com/ZiZc3/XPSemu/blob/8eec07b4e31f66dce8e0b05c1ca1281af303e933/util/compatfd.c#L28-L53)), which `qemu_signal_init` ([main-loop.c](https://github.com/ZiZc3/XPSemu/blob/8eec07b4e31f66dce8e0b05c1ca1281af303e933/util/main-loop.c#L110-L147)) starts for `SIGIO`, `SIGALRM` and `SIGBUS` when the main loop is created, so it reaches the wait at start-up, and from the vCPU thread of the dummy accelerator ([dummy-cpus.c](https://github.com/ZiZc3/XPSemu/blob/8eec07b4e31f66dce8e0b05c1ca1281af303e933/accel/dummy-cpus.c#L48-L56)). `sigsuspend` swaps the process-wide mask of `_sigprocmask` for its argument, waits as `pause` does through the same helper, then restores the mask through `_sigprocmask`, and returns -1 with `EINTR`; a null set throws, as the console faults in libthr instead of returning `EFAULT`. All four words of the argument replace the mask and are restored afterwards, as in `_sigprocmask`. Java 25 LAN / DNS (PPSA99869, #5501) imports it and fails to load without it, after `sysctlnametomib`, `fegetenv` and `mincore`. None of the five waits is a cancellation point

name: libkernel.L155
text: [sceKernelRaiseException](../../../core/libs/prx/libkernel/System/src/Exception.cpp) on Windows suspends the target and redirects it to the handler. A target running host code (any module other than the executable and the `*.guest.prx` modules, so libkernel, libc and the other HLE modules count too) is resumed and sampled again until it is back in guest code, since a handler that waits there would keep the host locks that code holds; a target blocked in an ntdll wait is redirected in place, as are NtContinue and winpthreads after their retry limit. A target that stays in host code without waiting for 50 ms after the raise began, such as a long HLE or driver call, is then redirected in host code anyway, with the same hazard. A target seen right after a `syscall` instruction in ntdll, inside a system call that is not a wait such as the `NtWriteFile` of an `fwrite` holding its stream lock, restarts those 50 ms, so a raise can cost the raising thread up to the 1 s retry limit. While the target is suspended only `VirtualQuery` and a lock-free cache of image bases are consulted; an image not yet in the cache is classified with `GetModuleFileNameW` after the target is resumed. An APC queued at the first host-code sample, which an alertable guest wait would run sooner, is not implemented
